rationale: The temple's bronze altar recalls the commanded bronze-covered altar. The source gives twenty by twenty by ten cubits, whereas Exodus gives five by five by three; these are different constructions, not matching dimensions.

relationship: Sea construction parallel with differing circumference
rationale: Both describe the round Sea as ten cubits across and five high. Chronicles gives a thirty-cubit circumference and Kings thirty-three; the difference is preserved.

Both place encircling features beneath the Sea. Chronicles calls them likenesses of calves and describes their casting in two groups; Kings calls them supports beneath the brim and gives a different formulation of their spacing.

Both put twelve bovine figures beneath the Sea in four groups of three. Chronicles says west and hindquarters inward, while Kings says toward the sea and hindquarters toward the house; the descriptions remain distinct.
Both describe a cup-like rim, lily imagery, and a hand-sized thickness. Chronicles additionally states a capacity of three thousand metretes, which this Kings unit does not supply.

The ten basins and their five-on-each-side arrangement correspond to Kings' ten basins on ten stands divided between the house's sides. Only Chronicles here explains the separate washing functions of basins and Sea.

Chronicles assigns the Sea to priestly washing. Exodus commands a bronze basin for Aaron and his sons to wash before entering the tent or approaching the altar; the temple arrangement develops that washing function without equating the vessels.
Both describe gold lampstands placed five on the right and five on the left. Kings locates them before the inner sanctuary, while Chronicles expressly totals ten and mentions their ordinance.

The ten temple tables made here reappear in the chapter's vessel summary as tables bearing the bread of presentation. The connection supplies their stated function; the hundred bowls are an additional detail of this source unit.

Both record construction of the temple court. Kings describes stone courses and cedar; Chronicles names the priests' and great courts and bronze-covered doorways, without requiring an equation of each court subdivision.
Both place the Sea on the house's right side with an eastward orientation. Kings adds the southern slope, a qualification not stated in this Chronicles unit.

Both introduce a concluding inventory by reporting that the craftsman's work for Solomon in the Lord's house was finished. Their opening utensil lists differ, and the names remain Chiram here and Hiram in Kings.

Both inventories enumerate two pillars and two networks covering their upper ornaments. Chronicles retains the terms golath and chothareth; Kings describes twisted ornaments and carvings, without establishing a precise translation of those terms.

Both discuss ornaments on the two networks in paired rows or groups. Chronicles counts four hundred golden bells and also mentions pomegranates; Kings counts four hundred pomegranates. The counted objects are not equated.

Both list ten supporting structures with basins upon them. Chronicles calls the supports mechonoth and Kings calls them stands; the comparison rests on their stated number and basin-supporting arrangement.
Both summaries enumerate one Sea with twelve bovine figures beneath it, called calves here and cattle in Kings.

Both conclude a craftsman's temple inventory by describing vessels made for Solomon in bronze. Their individual utensil lists and Kings' added pillars differ, so the connection does not equate every listed object.
Both place the king's casting work in thick earth in the Jordan region. The local names differ as Sokchoth/Sirdatha here and Succoth/Sira in Kings; no independent place-name equation is claimed.
Both describe the enormous bronze supply behind Solomon's works in terms of weight. Chronicles says the supply did not run out; Kings says its abundance prevented a measured limit.

relationship: Gold altar and bread table parallel
rationale: Both list a gold altar and tables or a table carrying presentation bread among the temple vessels. Chronicles has plural tables and Kings one gold table; the difference is retained.

The bread of presentation upon the temple tables continues the commanded placing of the bread of the Presence on the table before the Lord. The reference concerns the bread's prescribed location and function.
Both list gold lampstands and lamps before the inner sanctuary, called the dabir in Chronicles. The source's ordinance language accompanies the same stated lighting equipment.

The temple lamps provide light according to an ordinance. Exodus prescribes continual lamp service outside the covenant veil, tended by Aaron and his sons; this is a specific antecedent for sanctuary lighting, not an assertion that the fixtures are identical.

Both inventories include gold lamps, bowls, and incense or fire-handling vessels. Their lists use different terms, so the comparison concerns the listed golden equipment without identifying every utensil one for one.
Both closing inventories mention the Holy of Holies entrance and gold doors of the temple house. Kings also names doorframes and other fittings absent from this source unit.
Both report completion of Solomon's temple work and deposit of David's consecrated silver, gold, and vessels in the temple treasury. Kings also mentions Solomon's consecrated things.
Both have Solomon assemble Israel's elders to bring the covenant ark from the City of David, explicitly identified as Zion. Chronicles expands the classes of leaders summoned.

The temple-transfer assembly is dated by month in both accounts. Chronicles says the feast in the seventh month; Kings names Athanin without an ordinal here, so no independent calendar-name equivalence is imposed.

Both describe the carrying of the ark at the assembly. Chronicles identifies the bearers as Levites and Kings as priests; the reference preserves those descriptions rather than substituting one for the other.
Both include the Tent of Testimony and its holy vessels in the transfer alongside the ark. Chronicles additionally specifies priests and Levites as those bringing them up.
Both place Solomon and Israel before the ark sacrificing cattle and sheep too numerous to count. Chronicles adds descriptions of those assembled around the king.
Both describe priests bringing the covenant ark into the house's inner sanctuary, the Holy of Holies, beneath the cherubim's wings.
Both describe spread cherubim wings covering the ark from above. Chronicles explicitly names carrying poles among what is covered; Kings uses the broader wording holy things.

Both say projecting ends were visible from the holy places before the inner sanctuary but not from outside. Chronicles specifies carrying poles, whereas Kings calls the objects consecrated things; the object terminology remains distinct.
Both state that the ark contained only the two tablets Moses placed there at the covenant associated with the exodus. The location is written Choreb here and Horeb in Kings.

The source remembers Moses placing the covenant tablets in the ark. Deuteronomy narrates the replacement tablets, their divine writing, and Moses' placement of them in the ark, without making the later claim that nothing else was inside.
Both introduce the cloud episode as the priests emerge from the holy place. Chronicles adds their sanctification and the absence of course arrangement; those details are not supplied by Kings.

Both describe temple hymn singers using cymbals, nablai, and kinyrai in family-based service. The earlier text supplies the musical organization, while this source adds linen clothing and one hundred twenty trumpeting priests; differing personal spellings are not independently resolved.

Chronicles places the house-filling cloud after united musical thanksgiving. Kings likewise describes the cloud filling the house and identifies it with the Lord's glory, without supplying the musical scene.
Both call for thanksgiving to the Lord and ground it in His enduring mercy. Chronicles says it is good, while the psalm says He is kind; the shared refrain is retained with that wording difference.
Both state that the priests could not stand to minister because the cloud and the Lord's glory filled the house.

The house filled with glory prevents priestly ministry, recalling the cloud-filled tent that Moses could not enter. The settings and affected ministers differ, while the manifestation and its immediate effect closely correspond.

Solomon's statement that the Lord would dwell in thick darkness corresponds to the complete Kings unit's saying about dwelling in gloom. Kings places the saying after the prayer and includes the sun, a building command, and the Book of Song notice.

Both sayings connect the completed house with divine dwelling. Chronicles speaks of a house holy to the Lord and ready throughout the ages; the complete Kings unit speaks of building a splendid house and dwelling in newness, without equating the differing formulations.
Both depict the king turning his face and blessing Israel while the assembly stands.
Both bless Israel's God for fulfilling by His hands what He had spoken concerning David with His mouth.
Both recall that since the exodus the Lord had chosen no tribal city for a house bearing His name. Chronicles additionally states that no man had been chosen as leader at that stage.
Both explicitly state the choices of Jerusalem for the Lord's name and David over Israel. Kings combines these choices with the preceding no-city statement in one unit.
Both report David's heartfelt intention to build a house for the name of the Lord, Israel's God.
Both have the Lord commend David because building a house for His name had come into David's heart.
Both distinguish David's intention from the commission: David will not build the house, but the son coming from his body will build it for the Lord's name.

Solomon's speech recalls the promise that David's bodily offspring would build the house. The earlier oracle announces that offspring and the building task, together with the establishment of his throne.
Both identify Solomon's succession to David's throne and construction of the house as establishment of the Lord's spoken word.
Both declare that the completed house received the ark containing the Lord's covenant. Kings further recalls the fathers' exodus from Egypt.
Both place Solomon before the Lord's altar and Israel's assembly with hands spread out. Kings specifies heavenward direction in this unit; Chronicles supplies that direction in the following unit.

Chronicles describes Solomon kneeling with hands spread toward heaven on a bronze platform. Kings recalls the same kneeling and hand posture as he rises after prayer; the platform and its dimensions occur only in Chronicles here.
Both begin the prayer by affirming that no god compares with Israel's God in heaven or earth and by praising His covenant mercy toward wholehearted servants.
Both address God as having fulfilled for David, by His hands on this day, the promise spoken by His mouth.
Both ask that David's line continue on Israel's throne provided his sons guard their ways and walk faithfully. Chronicles explicitly says walking in God's law; Kings says walking before Him.
Both ask the Lord to confirm the word spoken to David, the speaker's father.
Both ask whether God will dwell with people on earth and confess that even heaven and the heaven of heaven cannot contain or suffice for Him, much less the built house.
Both ask the Lord to attend to His servant's prayer on this day. Chronicles calls it supplication; Kings also describes rejoicing offered in prayer.
Both ask that God's eyes remain open toward the house day and night because His name is associated with that place, so that the servant's prayer toward it is heard.
Both seek a hearing for the servant and Israel when they pray toward the house, asking God to hear from His heavenly dwelling and show mercy.
Both introduce the case of a person sinning against a neighbor and taking an oath-curse before the altar in this house.
Both ask God to hear from heaven, judge, return the lawless person's way upon his head, and vindicate the righteous according to righteousness.
Both envision Israel defeated before enemies because of sin, then returning, acknowledging God's name, and praying in the house.
Both ask God to hear from heaven, forgive Israel's sins, and return the people to the land given to their fathers.
Both describe heaven shut without rain because of sin, followed by prayer toward this place, acknowledgment of God's name, and turning from sin under His humbling.
Both ask for heavenly hearing and mercy, instruction in the good way, and rain upon the land given to the people as inheritance.
Both enumerate famine, death, crop afflictions, locusts, and enemy pressure as occasions for prayer. The lists' individual agricultural terms differ and are not made identical.

Both describe individual prayer arising from recognized affliction and hands spread toward the house. Chronicles includes personal weakness and all Israel; Kings speaks of the affliction of one's heart.
Both ask God to hear from His heavenly dwelling, show mercy, and deal with each person according to his ways, because God alone knows human hearts.
Both state the prayer's purpose as enduring reverence during life in the land given to the fathers. Chronicles says fear Thy ways, while Kings says fear Thee.

Both extend the prayer to a foreigner outside Israel who prays toward this place. Chronicles supplies the distant land and God's great name, mighty hand, and uplifted arm, details absent from these Kings units.
Both ask God to answer the foreigner's invocation so that the earth's peoples know and fear His name and recognize that His name is called over the house.
Both describe Israel going to battle by God's directed way and praying toward the chosen city and the house built for His name.
Both ask God to hear the people's supplication and prayer from heaven and uphold their cause or right.
Both affirm that no human is without sin and envisage divine judgment handing Israel to captors who deport them to a land far or near.
Both describe captives turning their hearts and pleading with God in exile, confessing sin, wrongdoing, and lawlessness, with the confession's terms ordered differently.
Both describe return with the whole heart and soul in the captors' land and prayer toward the ancestral land, chosen city, and house built for God's name.
Solomon's prayer envisages the wholehearted return of exiles. Deuteronomy likewise places return with all heart and soul among the nations of dispersion and promises mercy and regathering.
Both ask God to hear from His prepared heavenly dwelling and forgive the exiled people's sins. Chronicles also asks for judgments; Kings adds compassion before their captors.
Both conclude with a request that God's eyes and ears attend to supplication. Chronicles focuses on this place; Kings explicitly names the servant and Israel.

Both call the Lord to arise to His rest with the ark and pair clothed priests with rejoicing worshippers. Chronicles says ark of strength and salvation, while the psalm says ark of holiness and righteousness.

The prayer that priests be clothed with salvation has a close counterpart in the psalm's promise to clothe priests with salvation. Both add rejoicing, with Chronicles naming sons and the psalm holy ones.
Both ask that the anointed one's face not be turned away and appeal to David. Chronicles asks remembrance of David's mercies; the psalm says for David's sake.

Both dedication scenes join divine glory with fire consuming whole burnt offerings. Chronicles says fire came from heaven after Solomon's prayer; Leviticus says fire came from the Lord after Moses and Aaron emerged and blessed the people.

The priests cannot enter the house because the Lord's glory fills it, recalling Moses' inability to enter the cloud-filled Tent of Testimony. The connection preserves the different sanctuary and minister.
In both scenes the people see divine fire consume the offering and fall on their faces. Chronicles additionally locates them on stone pavement and records their praise of enduring mercy.
Both describe the king and all Israel offering sacrifices before the Lord at the temple dedication.
Both give twenty-two thousand bovine animals and one hundred twenty thousand flock animals or sheep at the dedication of the Lord's house by Solomon and the people.

The priests' trumpets and Levitical instruments accompanying thanksgiving here correspond to the earlier dedication scene with instrumental singers and priests sounding trumpets. Both preserve the refrain of enduring mercy, while this unit explicitly associates the songs with David.

Both explain that Solomon consecrated the court's middle for offerings because the bronze altar could not accommodate them. The offering lists differ, including Chronicles' untranslated manaa, which is not silently assigned an equivalent.

Both describe Solomon and a great Israelite assembly keeping the feast for seven days, bounded by a northern entrance and an Egyptian watercourse. The place spellings and torrent-versus-river wording remain distinct.

Chronicles associates an eighth-day closing celebration with seven days of altar dedication. Kings describes a seven-day feast and dismissal on the eighth day; the notices are compared without constructing a harmonized calendar.

Both dismiss the people to their homes rejoicing over God's goodness to David and Israel. Chronicles dates dismissal to the twenty-third of the seventh month and also names Solomon; Kings says the eighth day without that calendar date.
Both report completion of the Lord's house, the royal house, and the undertakings Solomon desired. Chronicles adds that these undertakings prospered.

Both describe God appearing to Solomon after the building and acknowledging his prayer and the chosen or consecrated house. Chronicles specifies night and a house of sacrifice; Kings calls this the second appearance.
God's warning about withheld rain, locusts, and death answers calamities named in Solomon's dedication prayer. The response selects these particular afflictions from the prayer's longer list.

God's promise to hear repentant prayer, forgive sins, and heal the land answers Solomon's requests for hearing and mercy when Israel returns after defeat or drought. The response adds seeking His face and being ashamed.
God's promise of open eyes and attentive ears to prayer in this place directly answers Solomon's request using those same bodily images and the same place-focused supplication.
Both promise that God's name will remain at the consecrated house for ever and that His eyes and heart will be there continually.
Both condition the royal promise on walking before God as David did and keeping divine commands and ordinances. Kings additionally specifies holiness of heart and uprightness.
Both promise to establish Solomon's throne according to the word to David that a ruler in Israel would not be removed from his line.
Both warn against abandoning divine commandments and ordinances to serve and worship other gods. Kings explicitly addresses the king and his children and mentions Moses.

Both threaten removal from the given land and rejection of the sanctified house. Chronicles makes the house a parable and tale; Kings says Israel becomes a disappearance and subject of talk, so those subjects are not merged.
Both imagine passersby astonished at the lofty house and asking why the Lord has treated the land and house this way. Kings adds hissing.
Both answer that abandonment of the God who brought the people or fathers from Egypt, followed by service and worship of other gods, caused the calamity.
Both open this phase with the twenty years during which Solomon built the Lord's house and his own royal house.

Chronicles says Chiram gave Solomon cities that Solomon rebuilt and settled. Kings describes Solomon giving Hiram cities that displeased their recipient. The reversed direction and different outcomes are retained without inventing a return transaction.

The named wilderness building and fortified cities here lead into the chapter's broader summary of Solomon's fortified, chariot, and cavalry cities. The link situates these particular works within that construction catalogue without identifying differently named places.

The account specifies walls, gates, and bars for Upper and Lower Baithoron before broadening to Solomon's fortified-city works. The adjacent summary supplies the wider construction setting, not additional fortification details for these two cities.

Both describe Solomon's chariot cities, horsemen or cavalry cities, and desired building works in Jerusalem and across his realm. Their additional named places differ and are not made interchangeable.

Both identify non-Israelite peoples remaining in the land before explaining their tribute status. The lists overlap in narrative function but differ in spellings and membership; Kings adds Canaanites and Girgashites.
Both describe descendants left in the land whom Israel had not destroyed and whom Solomon subjected to continuing tribute. Kings combines this explanation with its peoples list in one suffixed unit.
Both distinguish Israel's men from the subjected labor force, assigning them military and royal service, including chariot command and horsemen. The lists of offices are similar but not identical.

Both record chiefs overseeing Solomon's work. Chronicles gives two hundred fifty and Kings three thousand six hundred; these totals are not reconciled or assumed to enumerate exactly the same supervisory group.

Both describe Solomon bringing Pharaoh's daughter up from the City of David to a built house. Chronicles says he built it for her and gives an ark-related holiness reason; Kings says the house was built for himself.

Solomon now offers whole burnt offerings on the altar he built before the sanctuary. The earlier construction notice records his bronze altar and dimensions, providing the temple-building antecedent for this later use.
Chronicles explicitly invokes Moses' command and names three annual feast seasons. Deuteronomy prescribes the same three: Unleavened Bread, Weeks, and Tents, with attendance at the chosen place.

relationship: Sabbath and new-moon offering law connection
rationale: The source includes Sabbath and monthly offerings within Moses' prescribed schedule. Numbers specifically commands Sabbath whole burnt offerings and offerings at new moons; these support those parts of the source's schedule.

Solomon stations priestly divisions according to service under David's ordinance. The earlier organization of priestly divisions describes their entry and ministry in the Lord's house according to the commanded ordinance.

The source assigns gatekeepers by division at each gate following David's arrangement. The earlier gatekeeper organization describes service courses and lots for each gate, directly illuminating that portion of the installation.

The statement that priests and Levites did not transgress the king's commands follows the preceding specification of their service divisions, watches, and gate assignments. It reports adherence to those arrangements and also mentions treasuries.

Both summarize the temple project from foundation to completion. Kings supplies the fourth- and eleventh-year dates and months; Chronicles here supplies no dates and emphasizes that all the work was prepared.

Both locate Solomon's maritime activity on a coast in a southern territory, with paired port names. Chronicles writes Gasion-gaber, Ailath, and Idumean land; Kings writes Ezion-geber, Elath, and Edom. The comparison does not independently prove those place-name equations.

relationship: Maritime expedition parallel with differing gold total
rationale: Both describe experienced sailors joining Solomon's servants for a voyage to Sophira and returning gold to him. Chronicles gives four hundred fifty talents and Kings one hundred twenty; the totals are left unreconciled.

Both describe a queen testing Solomon with riddles and arriving in Jerusalem with camels, spices, abundant gold, and precious stones to discuss all in her heart or soul. Her name is written Saba here and Sheba in Kings.
Both say Solomon explained all the queen's matters, with none escaping or being overlooked by him.
Both introduce the queen's astonishment through her sight of Solomon's wisdom or discernment and the house he had built.

Both list food, servants' seating, ministers' stations, clothing, wine-pourers, and temple burnt offerings as the sight that overwhelmed the queen. The clothing details differ and are not assigned to identical persons in both lists.
Both have the queen affirm that the report heard in her own land about Solomon's words and wisdom or discernment was true.

Both contrast the queen's initial unbelief with what her own eyes saw and say that not even half had been reported. Chronicles emphasizes abundant wisdom; Kings speaks of added good things beyond the report.
Both pronounce those continually standing before Solomon and hearing his wisdom blessed. Chronicles also says happy men, whereas Kings opens with blessed women; that difference is preserved.

Both bless God for delighting in Solomon and making him king out of love for Israel, to establish righteous judgment. Chronicles calls the throne God's and Solomon king for God; Kings calls it Israel's throne.
Both record one hundred twenty talents of gold, precious stones, and an unparalleled supply of spices given by the visiting queen to Solomon.

Both connect gold from Souphir with timber and precious stones. Chronicles identifies servants and pinewood, while Kings identifies Hiram's ship and unhewn wood; the timber descriptions are not silently equated.

Both describe imported wood used for the Lord's and royal houses and for singers' instruments. Chronicles says pinewood stairways, while Kings says unhewn-wood supports; their different architectural and material descriptions remain intact.

Both say Solomon granted the queen her desires and requests before she returned to her land. Chronicles' additional clause concerns what she brought to Solomon; Kings' clause concerns what he had given her, and the direction is preserved.
Both give the gold arriving in one year as six hundred sixty-six talents.

Both add tribute and merchant revenue, kings, and satraps beyond the annual gold total. Chronicles specifies Arabia's kings and gold and silver, whereas Kings says kings of the region beyond without those metals in this unit.

Both catalogue Solomon's hammered-gold military display pieces, but Chronicles has two hundred large shields using six hundred gold pieces each, while Kings has three hundred spears using three hundred each. Objects and numbers are not equated.

Both record three hundred hammered-gold shields stored in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Chronicles gives three hundred gold pieces per shield; Kings gives three minas, without a supplied conversion.
Both describe Solomon's great ivory throne overlaid or gilded with tested gold; Chronicles explicitly mentions tusks.
Both give six steps, side armrests, and two lions beside the arms. Chronicles mentions gold fastening and Kings calf foreparts behind the throne, details not exchanged between the descriptions.
Both place twelve lions on the six steps, on either side, and declare the arrangement unmatched in other kingdoms.

relationship: Golden vessels and silver valuation parallel
rationale: Both describe gold royal vessels and gold-covered vessels in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, with silver considered of no account in Solomon's days. Kings further specifies drinking vessels and basins.

Both describe royal shipping associated with Chiram or Hiram and a three-year arrival cycle carrying gold and silver. Chronicles' tusks and apes differ from Kings' engraved and hewn stones; the cargo lists and Tharsis/Tarshish spellings are preserved.
Both say Solomon surpassed the other kings in wealth and wisdom or discernment.
Both say earth's kings sought Solomon's presence to hear the wisdom or discernment God had put in his heart.
Both list yearly gifts of gold vessels, clothing, stacte, spices, horses, and mules. Chronicles also includes silver vessels, absent from this Kings list.
Both give four thousand mares for chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, stationed in chariot cities and with Solomon in Jerusalem. The comparison keeps mares as the counted object.
Both describe rule over kings from the River to the foreigners' land and Egypt's border. The Kings connection is the actual suffixed unit 26a.
Both liken Jerusalem's gold and silver to stones and its cedar abundance to sycamores in the plain.
Both identify Egypt as a source of Solomon's horses. Chronicles also says all the land; Kings names Thekoue and the merchants' exchange, which are not substituted for that broader wording.
Both direct readers to written records for Solomon's remaining acts. Chronicles names prophetic records and visions, while Kings names the Book of Solomon's Acts; the cited works are not equated.
Both give Solomon a forty-year reign. Chronicles specifies all Israel, and Kings locates the reign in Jerusalem.
Both report Solomon's death, burial in David's city, and succession by Rehoboam his son. The complete Kings unit additionally recounts Jeroboam's return from Egypt and repeats Solomon's death notice.
Both have Rehoboam go to the city where all Israel assembled to make him king. The place is written Sychem in Chronicles and Shechem in Kings.

Both recall Jeroboam's flight from Solomon and residence in Egypt before his return. The complete Kings unit places the return in the death-and-succession notice and specifies his destination; Chronicles places it before the assembly's appeal.
Both introduce the people's address to Rehoboam. Chronicles explicitly includes the summons and Jeroboam with Israel's assembly; the shorter Kings unit identifies only the people speaking.
Both ask Rehoboam to relieve his father's harsh service and heavy burden, promising service in return. Chronicles calls it a yoke and Kings a collar.
Both have the king send the petitioners away for three days and command them to return.
Both describe Rehoboam consulting the elders who served his living father Solomon about how to answer the people.
Both advise good words and favorable treatment to secure enduring service. Chronicles says be good and show favor; Kings explicitly tells the king to become the people's servant and serve them.
Both report that Rehoboam abandoned the elders' counsel and consulted the young men raised with him who stood before him.
Both have Rehoboam ask the young men how to answer the people's request for a lighter paternal burden, described as a yoke here and a collar in Kings.

Both have the young men propose a boast contrasting the king's small part with his father's loins. Chronicles explicitly says little finger, while Kings says little part, so the anatomical wording is not silently standardized.
Both advise promising a heavier burden and contrasting the father's whips with the son's scorpions. Chronicles says yoke and Kings collar.
Both place the people's return on the third day according to the king's command. Chronicles specifically names Jeroboam among those returning.
Both describe the king's harsh answer and his abandonment of the elders' advice.
Both show Rehoboam delivering the younger advisers' threat to increase the inherited burden and replace whips with scorpions; the source uses yoke and Kings collar.

Both explain the king's refusal to listen as a divine turn establishing the prophetic word concerning Jeroboam. The names remain Achia the Selonite and Nabat here, Ahijah the Shilonite and Nebat in Kings, without independent name-equivalence claims.

Both connect the king's refusal with Israel's cry denying a share in David and Jesse's son and returning to their dwellings or tents. Chronicles begins by continuing the preceding divine-word sentence; that opening is preserved as part of the complete source unit.

Chronicles specifies Rehoboam's rule over Israelites living in Judah's cities. Kings' later retelling says Judah and Benjamin followed him to Jerusalem; it supports the retained southern allegiance without equating those population descriptions.
Both describe the king sending Adoniram over the tribute, Israel stoning him to death, and Rehoboam escaping to Jerusalem. Chronicles explicitly mentions mounting the chariot.
Both close the episode by stating that Israel rejected David's house, continuing to the narrator's present day.
